STOCKHOLM, Oct 15 : Telecom gear maker Ericsson on Thursday reported a smaller-than-expected drop in third-quarter core profit as efficiency measures helped offset higher component costs, but warned that such costs would affect margins next year.  • Operating profit before amortisation and restructuring costs was 10.1 billion crowns ($1.01 billion) against a year-earlier 15.8 billion and a mean forecast of 7.87 billion in a poll of analysts provided by Ericsson • The Swedish group said component costs rose in the quarter • "Looking ahead, the RAN (Radio Access Network) market is flat, geopolitical uncertainty remains elevated and component costs are a headwind to gross margin," new CEO Per Narvinger said in a statement

Oct 15 : Dutch digital mapping specialist TomTom NV said on Thursday it would cut 200 jobs globally as part of a reorganisation expected to generate annualised savings of about €21 million ($23.6 million). The company, which has been investing lately in its new mapping platform, TomTom Orbis, is gradually shifting its focus towards partnerships to develop new driving solutions, working with Microsoft on generative AI and with Mitsubishi Electric on automated driving, among others. "We see significant growth opportunities in automated driving and location intelligence, driven by AI," CEO Mike Schoofs said in a statement. TomTom raised its 2026 operating margin guidance to around 4 per cent from 3 per cent previously, including the impact of a €15 million restructuring charge in the fourth quarter.

BENGALURU, Oct 15 : Figma's CFO said on Thursday it was uncertain if the design software firm would return to peak gross margin levels as it ramps up AI spending, but said the investments will help draw users and better compete with sophisticated tools from labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. The company has been spending heavily on AI features, including its Figma design assistant and tools that can create prototypes and web applications using text prompts, which have helped drive a steady surge in revenue, but weighed on margins. "Are we going to get back to the low-90s gross margin percentage? I don't know. But is that the thing I would be acutely focused on? No," CFO Praveer Melwani told the Reuters Global Markets Forum on the sidelines of the company's Config user conference in Bengaluru, India. Figma's quarterly gross profit margins have shrunk to the mid-80 per cent range over the past year, down from above 90 per cent historically.

The company is betting that sacrificing margins now to boost AI adoption will help expand its user base and eventually give it room to raise prices. Figma earlier this year moved to a usage-based pricing model for AI credits on its platform. The monetization effort is expected to deliver stronger earnings in the upcoming quarters. Investors, however, have been scrutinizing finances at tech companies as they assess the returns on costly AI bets. Those concerns, coupled with worries over AI-driven disruptions, have dragged Figma's stock down about 43 per cent this year. "I would be willing to take the hit on margin the same way that we did over the last year if it means that we're able to serve a much larger total addressable market," Melwani said. "What may be good for us may not always be what an investor is looking for... We know we're going to have the ability to take price at the right point." At Config India, Figma announced expanded access to its code layers tool, new collaborative features, and partnerships with agent platforms including OpenCode, Meta Muse and India's Sarvam AI. NEW DELHI, Oct 15 : West Indies captain Shai Hope is worried he may have to fork out excess baggage fees after picking up his third Player of the Match award on their tour of India. The opener's unbeaten 102 in the fourth Twenty20 International on Wednesday set up a series-levelling win in Hyderabad. He also smashed a century in the second T20 in Ranchi. Hope has been in sizzling form throughout the tour, hitting two hundreds in the earlier One-Day International leg. And while he was pleased with his performances he said he was struggling to fit his awards in his luggage. "To be honest, they are a bit heavy, and we have got to look at the luggage weight," he quipped after West Indies prevailed by 24 runs.

"So it was good for us to start innings and then obviously we got that foundation, you can express yourself a bit more in the middle period and then try to give the team the best finish as could as possible." "He has been playing some really good cricketing shots, not taking that much risk, and respecting the bowlers as well." FAST

BANGKOK, Oct 15 : Prolonged war in the Middle East and further disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies in the Middle East and Central Asia, the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday. Jihad Azour, the IMF's director for the Middle East and Central Asia, told reporters the war was imposing a highly uneven economic shock to the broader region, with directly affected states under severe pressure. "The outlook depends critically on how quickly energy production and trade normalize, and on countries’ ability to preserve macroeconomic stability," Azour said at a news conference during the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. Pre-war surpluses, alternative routes, demand adjustments and substantial inventory drawdowns had helped contain the impact of the energy shock caused by the US-Israeli-led attacks on Iran and Tehran's subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

"These buffers bought time, but they are finite. Inventories are lower, spare capacity is tighter, and renewed disruption could generate much larger price adjustments," he said. The global lender is forecasting a deep contraction of 1.3 per cent in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan region after growth of 3.3 per cent in 2025, followed by a strong, but uneven rebound in 2027, when growth is expected to hit 6.6 per cent, Azour said, noting substantial differences across the region. Oil-exporting countries directly affected by the war would see a significant contraction in 2026 and a sharp rebound in growth in 2027 as energy production normalizes, but output was expected to remain below pre-war medium-term projections. The economies of oil-importing countries in the region had been resilient and were expected to remain so, he said. The Caucasus and Central Asia region had weathered the shock relatively well and inflation was expected to continue declining from elevated levels. The IMF is projecting growth to slow to 5.2 per cent in 2026 and then 5 per cent in 2027, from growth of 6.2 per cent in 2025. Azour said policymakers should prioritize price stability, focus on rebuilding fiscal buffers and expand their capacity to withstand future shocks.

Source: Reuters

FAST

TOKYO, Oct 15 : Some of Japan's largest asset managers are expected to unveil plans to buy more domestic bonds with markets focusing on whether they would step up divestments of overseas assets to bring money back home. Although a major reallocation is unexpected, consistent flows home could put a floor under the yen, analysts say, and would come at a time when shifts in Japanese demand are being closely watched because they can move foreign markets. A possible repatriation of some of the large amounts of capital deployed overseas has been under the spotlight in recent months as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government scrambled to shore up the yen, which dropped to a 40-year low in July. Japanese life insurers manage about $2.5 trillion in assets, about a quarter of which is held overseas, according to the Life Insurance Association of Japan. Several firms have lately signalled that they were eyeing domestic bonds as yields surged.

"I don't believe there is a trend toward repatriation in terms of divesting from foreign bonds to buy JGBs right now," said Keita Matsumoto, head of financial markets at SMBC Nikko Securities. "(Life insurers) are cautiously increasing their exposure to JGBs ... Their approach remains one of buying on dips as yields rise." Ministry of Finance figures show Japanese investors have made net foreign bond sales topping 5 trillion yen ($32 billion) this year, about 289 billion yen worth of which came from life insurers. In Japan, 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) yields, which until little more than two years ago were capped by the central bank, have tripled to soar past 3 per cent for the first time in three decades. Domestic insurers may also step up buying 30-year JGBs as yields consolidate around 4 per cent, while increases in hedge ratios may be a precursor to selling foreign bonds, said Shoki Omori, Deutsche Bank's chief fixed-income strategist for Japan. "They will stay measured while the BOJ is still raising rates," Omori said. "Some will let hedged foreign bonds run off as they mature. What I do not expect is a broad move to sell foreign bonds and bring the money back into yen."   "Higher yields have brought the buyers back to JGBs," he added. "They have not brought the money home." 'TOO EARLY TO STEP IN' Nippon Life, Meiji Yasuda Life and Daiichi Life, which collectively manage nearly 220 trillion yen in assets, are among insurers that are expected to unveil their investment plans next week. Inflation, rising sovereign debt and growth expectations boosted by the AI boom have driven yields sharply higher across the developed world this year. In Japan, Takaichi's spending plans and tax-cut pledge have also added to market concerns. A year ago, major Japanese life insurers flagged that they expected to trim their yen-denominated bond holdings and subsequent rises in yields across the curve indicate the market has not found a bottom yet. Japanese institutions that slashed JGB holdings during the negative-interest-rate era are embarking on a gradual reappraisal of their home market, said Tetsuji Hayashi, a product specialist in Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management's investment department. "We are starting to see a shift back toward yen bonds," Hayashi said. "As interest rates rise, the 10-year JGB yield has surpassed the FX-hedged 10-year US Treasury yield." The Bank of Japan raised its key rate to a 31-year high last month and many analysts expect the central bank to raise interest rates again by the end of this year amid persistent concerns over broadening price pressures and yen weakness. Worries about supply-and-demand dynamics remain across the JGB spectrum as the BOJ reduces its bond holdings and tightens policy while the country's finances remain shaky, said an asset management official at a major life insurance company. Bond yields in Japan have risen to "fairly attractive levels," but they have yet to peak, said the official, who asked not to be identified as they were not authorised to speak to the media. "It is still too early to step in," the official said. "The Bank of Japan is not done raising rates, and fiscal concerns have not cleared up either." ($1 = 158.2900 yen)

(Additional reporting by Noriyuki Hirata. Writing by Tom Westbrook; Editing by Sumeet Chatterjee and Thomas Derpinghaus)

Source: Reuters
